# Ray Traversal Schemes

Also called: Accumulate Projection, Depth Projection, Max Intensity Projection, Ray Traversal -Accumulate

## Overview
Ray traversal schemes define how scalar voxel values are aggregated along a ray to produce a final pixel intensity, ranging from simple statistical projections to physically-based compositing [S1, S2, S3, unofficial]. They solve the problem of mapping 3D volumetric data to 2D image space by determining which voxel properties (intensity, opacity, depth) contribute to the final pixel color [S2, unofficial]. Unlike [Ray Marching and Discretization](2788-ray-marching-and-discretization.md), which focuses on the spatial sampling of the ray, these schemes focus on the mathematical aggregation function applied to the sampled values [S2, unofficial]. They differ from [Monte Carlo Path Tracing for Volume Rendering](4980-monte-carlo-path-tracing-for-volume-rendering.md) by typically using deterministic, sequential accumulation rather than stochastic sampling [S4, unofficial].

## Shared principles
All ray traversal schemes operate on the samples generated by the ray marching process. For a ray intersecting the volume, a sequence of scalar values $d_i$ is obtained at discrete positions $t_i$ [S5, S10, unofficial]. The scheme defines a reduction function $F$ that maps the sequence $\{d_i\}$ to a single output value $I$ [S2, unofficial].

The most common aggregation types are defined by the following reduction functions, where $N$ is the number of samples along the ray [S2, unofficial]:

1.  **Intensity (First/Last)**: Selects the first or last non-background sample. Often used for iso-surface extraction [S1, unofficial].
    $$ I = d_{k} \quad \text{where } k = \min \{i \mid d_i \neq \text{background}\} $$
2.  **Max (Maximum Intensity Projection - MIP)**: Selects the maximum value along the ray. Useful for highlighting high-density structures like blood vessels in Magnetic Resonance Angiography [S2, S3, unofficial].
    $$ I = \max_{i=1 \dots N} (d_i) $$
3.  **Average**: Computes the arithmetic mean of all samples. Produces an X-ray-like projection where dense structures appear brighter [S1, S2, S3, unofficial].
    $$ I = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} d_i $$
4.  **Accumulate**: Combines color and opacity using front-to-back compositing. This is the standard for direct volume rendering, allowing transparent layers to be visible [S1, S3, unofficial]. It requires both a color $C_i$ and opacity $\alpha_i$ for each sample, derived from the scalar $d_i$ via a transfer function [S2, unofficial].

## Subtopics

### [Pixel Intensity Evaluation with Scene Aggregates](10890-pixel-intensity-evaluation-with-scene-aggregates.md)
Pixel Intensity Evaluation with Scene Aggregates is a method for evaluating pixel intensity by integrating radiance over a pixel footprint, using aggregated visibility functions to handle inter-voxel correlation and background blending without order-dependent ray marching [10890-pixel-intensity-evaluation-with-scene-aggregates]. It solves the problem of correctly blending scene aggregate contributions with external background objects by defining visibility on the 2D boundary enclosing a 3D scene aggregate [10890-pixel-intensity-evaluation-with-scene-aggregates]. It sets itself apart from its siblings by replacing sequential sample accumulation with a precomputed visibility integral that accounts for the geometric coverage of primitives within the pixel footprint [10890-pixel-intensity-evaluation-with-scene-aggregates].

### Voxel Aggregation Methods
Differentiable voxel aggregation methods treat ray traversal as a differentiable operation to enable gradient-based optimization of 3D structures from 2D images [S4, unofficial].

*   **Occupancy Probability (Yan et al.)**: Casts a ray from the pixel, samples all associated voxels, and chooses the one with the highest occupancy probability [S4, unofficial].
*   **Stopping Probability (Tulsiani et al.)**: Computes the probability that a ray stops at a certain distance, allowing rendering of depth maps, color images, and foreground masks [S4, unofficial].
*   **Bidirectional Emission-Absorption (Henzler et al.)**: Introduces a bidirectional emission-absorption (EA) light radiation model for emitting materials, in addition to visual hull (VH) and absorption-only (AO) models [S4, unofficial].
*   **Iterative Accumulation (Lombardi et al.)**: Casts a ray from each pixel and iteratively accumulates color and opacity probabilities. Discards remaining voxels when cumulative opacity reaches a maximum value to prevent further impact on color [S4, unofficial].
*   **Surface Localization (Jiang et al.)**: Casts a ray from the pixel and locates the surface voxel closest to the camera. Computes final pixel color as a weighted sum of the surface voxel and its neighboring voxels. Computes normal vector based on voxel values around the surface point for shading. Although locating the surface point is not a differentiable operation, the pixel color is differentiable with respect to the voxels around the surface point [S4, unofficial].

## Background
The term "Ray Traversal Schemes" encompasses a variety of projection and compositing techniques developed for Direct Volume Rendering (DVR). Early work by Tuy & Tuy (1984) introduced the "First" intensity scheme for iso-surface extraction [S1, unofficial]. The "Accumulate" scheme, popularized by Levoy (1988), established front-to-back compositing as the standard for visualizing transparent volumes [S1, S3, unofficial]. Maximum Intensity Projection (MIP) became a standard clinical tool for Magnetic Resonance Angiography [S2, S3, unofficial]. Recent developments in differentiable rendering have extended these schemes to support gradient-based optimization, treating ray traversal as a continuous operation over voxel probabilities [S4, unofficial].
